steps.note: g_hwnd starts as NULL: there is no window yet, so the ticket slot is empty. This program runs until you close it, so we film the set-up and one turn of the loop.
Windows starts the program at WinMain and hands it two things: hInst (this program) and nShow (how the window should first appear).
hPrev and lpCmd go unused, so the (void) casts tell the compiler that is on purpose.
A blank WNDCLASS form: the {0} sets every field to zero.
The key field: the address of WindowProc. Windows rings this function whenever something happens to the window.
hInstance says which program owns this kind of window.
The form gets a name: GameWindow.
RegisterClass hands the form to Windows, who files it under the name GameWindow.
CreateWindowEx orders a window of kind GameWindow, titled My First Window. It exists now, but nobody can see it yet.
WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW gives it a title bar, border and buttons. CW_USEDEFAULT means Windows picks where it goes.
The size is 800 by 600. The call returns a claim ticket, the HWND, and it is stored in g_hwnd.
ShowWindow makes the window visible, the way nShow asked.
msg is an empty box that will hold each message Windows sends.
GetMessage waits for something to happen. The first thing is a paint request, so a WM_PAINT message arrives.
DispatchMessage hands the message to the window's WindowProc.
WindowProc has no opinions yet, so it passes everything to DefWindowProc, Windows' own standard handling. The window paints itself.
Back to waiting. Only a quit message ends this loop and this version never gets one, so the program keeps running until you close it. We stop the film here.
The set-up from rung 1 hands Windows the address of WindowProc: this is the window's receptionist, with a row for each case. Later we pretend the user presses Esc.
CreateWindowEx builds the window. It is not visible yet.
ShowWindow shows it, and Windows drops a WM_PAINT envelope on the message queue: please paint yourself.
GetMessage picks the front envelope off the queue.
DispatchMessage carries the envelope to WindowProc. This is the moment Windows calls your function.
The switch looks at the message number. WM_PAINT is not one of our cases.
So it lands in default and goes to DefWindowProc, which paints the plain window.
GetMessage waits. Then the user presses Esc: a WM_KEYDOWN envelope arrives, with wp saying which key.
DispatchMessage carries it to WindowProc again.
This time the switch jumps to case WM_KEYDOWN.
wp is the Esc key, so DestroyWindow takes the window apart. Windows immediately sends WM_DESTROY straight back into WindowProc.
WindowProc is running again, and now the switch lands on case WM_DESTROY.
PostQuitMessage drops a WM_QUIT envelope on the queue. That is how the loop will learn it is time to stop.
return 0 tells Windows the message was handled.
GetMessage picks up WM_QUIT and returns 0 instead of a message. The while loop ends.
After the loop, msg.wParam holds the 0 we gave PostQuitMessage. It becomes the program's exit code.
msg is an empty box for incoming messages. A real game loop runs forever, so we film two frames and then pretend the user closes the window.
running is 1: the loop may go on.
The frame counter starts at 0.
A new frame begins. running is 1, so we go in.
PeekMessage glances at the queue. It is empty, so PeekMessage returns 0 at once. No waiting, so the game can carry on.
The frame itself: frame goes up by 1.
wsprintf writes the text Frame 1 into the title array.
SetWindowText puts that text in the title bar. You can see the loop running.
Sleep(16) rests for about 16 ms so the loop does not hog the CPU.
Next frame. While we slept, the user tapped a key, so an envelope is waiting. PeekMessage takes it and returns nonzero.
Is it WM_QUIT? No, it is WM_KEYDOWN, so running stays 1.
DispatchMessage hands the envelope to WindowProc, which passes it to DefWindowProc.
Ask again: the queue is empty now, so PeekMessage returns 0 and the inner loop ends.
Frame 2.
The title bar shows Frame 2.
Sleep(16) again.
Now the user closes the window. Closing ran WM_DESTROY in WindowProc, which called PostQuitMessage, so a WM_QUIT envelope is in the queue. PeekMessage finds it.
It is WM_QUIT, so running becomes 0. Unlike GetMessage, PeekMessage does not stop for you; you check for quit yourself.
The rest of this pass still runs. WM_QUIT belongs to no window, so Windows quietly drops it.
Queue empty again.
One last frame: frame goes to 3.
The title bar says Frame 3.
One last Sleep(16).
Back at the top, running is 0, so the loop ends.

do.t: running is 0: the game loop stops

steps.note: Return msg.wParam, the 0 from PostQuitMessage. The program exits.
g_rect_x is just a number: where the square should be. This program runs until closed, so we film the first paint and one arrow-key press.
A new window needs a first picture, so Windows queues a WM_PAINT. GetMessage picks it up.
DispatchMessage carries it to WindowProc.
case WM_PAINT: the one place we draw.
BeginPaint says "I am starting to draw" and gives us hdc, the surface to draw on.
FillRect with the window colour wipes the old picture clean first. Without this, old squares would smear.
SetRect works out where the square goes: 50 by 50 at g_rect_x.
CreateSolidBrush makes a green brush.
FillRect with the brush paints the square at 100.
We made the brush, so we delete it.
EndPaint finishes. The window now shows the square at 100.
Time passes. The user presses the Right arrow, and a WM_KEYDOWN envelope arrives.
DispatchMessage carries it to WindowProc.
case WM_KEYDOWN: an arrow key was pressed.
Is wp the Left arrow? No, so nothing happens here.
It is Right, so g_rect_x goes up by 5. The variable changed, but the window still shows the square at 100. The picture is out of date.
InvalidateRect hangs the wet paint sign: this picture needs redoing. Windows will send a WM_PAINT.
The next GetMessage picks up that WM_PAINT.
Dispatched to WindowProc.
BeginPaint starts drawing and clears the wet paint sign.
Wipe the old picture.
Paint the square at the new g_rect_x: 105. The painting matches the variable again.
EndPaint. Variables are the truth; the window is a painting of them, redone when we ask.
REM starts a comment, so this line does nothing. The picture: windows.h is a menu of every Windows function, and the .lib files are the kitchens that actually cook them.
First the compiler runs. The header (the menu) lists every function you call, so this step passes.
Then the linker, our waiter, walks every dish to a kitchen. user32.lib and gdi32.lib are both on the command line, so every dish has a kitchen.
Now imagine gdi32.lib is left off. The compile step still passes, because the menu lists the functions. The trouble comes at link time.
Unresolved external symbol: the linker was asked to call a function and cannot find its code anywhere.
steps.out: win32_window.obj : error LNK2019: unresolved external symbol

steps.note: The name looks odd, but strip the __imp__ in front and the @4 behind and you can read it: CreateSolidBrush. That is a gdi32 dish.
The summary line counts how many symbols were missing.
steps.out: win32_window.exe : fatal error LNK1120: 2 unresolved externals

steps.note: Two dishes had no kitchen: CreateSolidBrush and DeleteObject. The count is how many gdi32 functions your file calls. Add gdi32.lib and both are fixed.
Now the other way round: leave user32.lib off instead.
The same kind of error, but now the missing name is a user32 function. The A on the end of CreateWindowExA just means the plain-text version.

A window program has no console, so printf would print nowhere. AllocConsole opens one. This loop runs forever, so we film three frames. The ms numbers are samples from one run; yours will differ a little.
freopen points printf at that console.

do.t: printf now writes to the console

steps.note: Three variables for the stopwatch: freq, last and now. They are empty for now.
freq is how many ticks the counter makes each second. On this sample PC: 10 million. It never changes.
The first reading: the stopwatch starts here. The number alone means nothing; only differences between two readings do.
Frame 1: Sleep(16) is our old guess. The yellow dot is real time passing.
A second reading of the counter, taken right after the sleep.
now minus last is 168,213 ticks. Times 1000, divided by ticks per second, makes milliseconds: 16.8.
last = now. The end of this frame is the start of the next one.
printf writes the measured frame time.
Frame 2: sleep again.
Read the counter.
162,477 ticks make 16.2 ms. A little quicker this time.
last = now again.
Print the second frame time.
Frame 3: sleep.
Read the counter.
171,038 ticks make 17.1 ms. Sleep(16) was only a guess, and the stopwatch shows the real length.
last = now.
Print it. The loop would keep going until you close the window; we stop the film here.
g_rect_x is 100 and the window shows its square there. This program runs until closed, so we film one arrow-key press and the repaint it causes.
The user presses the Right arrow: a WM_KEYDOWN message reaches WindowProc.
g_rect_x becomes 105. The window still shows the old picture.
InvalidateRect asks for a repaint, so a WM_PAINT message follows.
case WM_PAINT: now we draw. This time, not straight onto the screen.
BeginPaint gives us hdc, the connection to the real window.
GetClientRect measures the drawable area: width and height. The numbers are used a few lines later.
CreateCompatibleDC makes a second drawing surface, back, that is not attached to the screen. It is backstage, behind the curtain.
CreateCompatibleBitmap makes the actual pixels for that backstage card: the same size as the window.
SelectObject puts the bitmap into back, so drawing on back goes onto the card. The old object it replaced is kept in old so we can undo this later.
Clear the card to the window colour. Only the hidden card changes; the audience still sees the old frame.
SetRect works out where the square goes on the card: x = 105.
A green brush.
Paint the square on the card at 105. The window on the left still shows 100: nobody has seen this half-finished work.
Done with the brush, so delete it.
BitBlt copies the finished card onto the window in one go. The curtain opens on a complete frame, never a half-drawn one.
Put the old object back into back, so the bitmap is no longer selected.
Delete the bitmap, because we made it. Skipping this leaks a bitmap every frame.
Delete the backstage drawing surface too.
EndPaint. The new frame is on screen, and the card is gone until the next paint.
